1. Checkmate wins, just like in chess. Mate in one!
2. Bare king: if you capture every enemy piece except the Shah, you win (unless your opponent can bare your Shah right back on the next move). Capture the last black piece!

3. You may give check with a dropped Pawn, but you may not checkmate by dropping a Pawn (uchifuzume). Here P@e8 would be mate, so it is against the rules and loses the game. Checkmate with a Pawn that moves is fine, and so is a mate by dropping any other piece.

Bikjang (said 'bick-jahng'): if the two Generals face each other on a file with nothing between them, the other player must break it right away. If not, the game ends and the pieces are counted. Here Cho has just moved to d2, so Han must react.
Black wins by capturing every white piece. White wins by checkmating the black King. Pawns move and promote as usual.
Castle early, usually in the first ten moves. Your king hides behind a wall of pawns, and your rook comes toward the center.
Castling is a special move that keeps your king safe. The king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook hops over to the other side of the king.
Checkmate means the king is in check and there is no way to escape. Checkmate wins the game!
Developing means moving your knights and bishops off the back row toward the center. Pieces at home do not help in the fight.
En passant (say "on pah-SAHN") is a sneaky pawn rule. If an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right next to your pawn, you can capture it as if it had moved only one square.
Italian Game. Play White: e4, Nf3 (attacks e5), Bc4 (aims at f7), then c3 to prepare d4 and build a big center.

Legal's Mate, a trap over 250 years old. Black pinned your knight with Bg4. Play Nc3. If Black plays ...g6, take on e5 with the "pinned" knight: Nxe5! If Black grabs your queen, finish with Bxf7+ and Nd5#.
Ruy Lopez. Play White: e4, Nf3, Bb5. When Black asks the bishop with ...a6, keep it with Ba4. Then castle and put the rook on e1 to guard e4.

Stalemate is a draw in sittuyin. Like makruk, there is also a counting rule: when one side has only its Min-gyi left and the other side has no pawns, the stronger side must mate within a limit (for example 16 moves with a Yahhta), or the game is drawn.
Stalemate: it is your turn, you are not in check, but you have no legal moves. That is a draw (a tie), even if you have fewer pieces!

64 squares and how to name them
A discovered check is the strongest kind: the uncovered piece gives check, so the moving piece can go anywhere and attack anything.
A double check happens when a moving piece gives check AND uncovers a second check. You cannot block two lines or capture two pieces at once, so the king must move. If it cannot, it is mate!
A fork is one piece attacking two or more enemy pieces at once. The opponent can only save one! Knights are the best forkers because their jumps are hard to see.
A pin attacks a piece that cannot move without exposing something more valuable behind it. Here the bishop pins the knight to the king. That is an absolute pin: moving the knight would be illegal.
A skewer is like a pin in reverse: you attack a valuable piece, it moves away, and you capture the piece behind it. Checks make the best skewers, because the king must move.
A Baidaq that reaches the last rank can only promote to a Ferz. Promote your Baidaq!
A Bia that reaches the sixth rank promotes at once into a Met (called Bia Ngai). Push your Bia!

A Ne can promote to a Sit-ke only if your Sit-ke has been captured. It must stand on one of the two long diagonals in the enemy half. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6, White's bishop has two famous homes. On c4 it aims at f7: that is the Italian Game. On b5 it pressures the knight that defends e5: that is the Ruy Lopez (or Spanish Game).
After it crosses the river it grows stronger: it may move one point forward or sideways. It can never move backward. It captures the same way it moves.
Against 1.e4, the Sicilian Defense 1...c5 is the most popular answer at top level. Black fights for d4 from the side and makes the game unbalanced.

Makruk (said 'mahk-rook') is the chess of Thailand. It is a close cousin of chess, but its pieces are slower and more careful, and the pawns start further forward. White moves first.

Makruk has counting rules so games cannot go on forever. When no unpromoted Bia are left, the weaker side may start counting, and the stronger side must checkmate within 64 moves. When the weaker side has only its Khun, the limit is shorter, for example 16 moves against one Rua or 8 against two. If the count runs out, the game is a draw. Shatranj (said 'shah-trahnj') was played in Persia and the Arab world more than 1000 years ago. It is the ancestor of modern chess. These are the rules as most historians reconstruct them.

Shogi (said 'show-gee') is the chess of Japan. Its big idea: pieces you capture join your army and can be dropped back onto the board. The first player is called Sente and sits at the bottom; the second player is Gote.

Silver, Knight, Lance and Pawn promote into pieces that move like a Gold (a promoted Pawn is called tokin, said 'toh-keen'). Rook becomes Dragon King, Bishop becomes Dragon Horse. The King and the Gold never promote. Promotion is your choice, but a captured promoted piece goes into the hand unpromoted.

Sittuyin (said 'sit-too-yin') is the chess of Myanmar (Burma). Its special feature: the players place their own pieces before the battle begins. The first player is shown at the bottom and moves first.

The Advisors are 仕 / 士 (shi, said 'shr'). In the picture set each is a scholar with a tall hat. An Advisor moves one point diagonally and must stay in the palace too, so it can only ever stand on these 5 points.
The Alfil (said 'al-feel', the elephant) jumps exactly two squares diagonally, leaping over whatever is in between. It can only ever visit 8 squares in the whole game!
The Baidaq (said 'bay-dahk', foot soldier) moves one square forward and captures one square diagonally forward, like a chess pawn. But it can never move two squares.
The Bia (said 'bee-ah') is the pawn, drawn as a pawn. It moves one square forward and captures one square diagonally forward. It never moves two squares, so there is no en passant.
The bishop moves diagonally, as far as it wants. A bishop stays on the same color square for the whole game!
The Cannon is 炮 / 砲 (pao, said 'pow'). In the picture set it is a cannon on wheels. When it is not capturing, it moves just like a Chariot: any distance in a straight line.

The Cannon 包 (po, said 'poh') is very different from the xiangqi cannon. In the picture set it is a cannon on wheels. It must always jump over exactly one piece, both to move and to capture. With no screen, it cannot move at all! Inside a palace it may also jump along a diagonal line, using a piece on the center point as its screen.

The Chariot is 俥 / 車 (ju, said 'jyoo'). In the picture set it is a two-wheeled war cart. It moves any number of points in a straight line, just like a rook in chess. It cannot jump over pieces. It is the strongest piece on the board!

The Chariot 車 (cha, said 'chah') is the strongest piece. In the picture set it is a two-wheeled war cart. It moves any distance in a straight line, and inside a palace it may also slide along the diagonal lines.

The Elephant is 相 / 象 (xiang, said 'shyahng'). In the picture set it is an elephant head. It moves exactly two points diagonally. It may not cross the river, so it can only use these 7 points. It is a defender.
The Elephant 象 (sang, said 'sahng') moves one point straight and then two points diagonally outward. In the picture set it is an elephant head. Unlike in xiangqi, it can go anywhere on the board.
The Ferz (said 'fairz', the counselor) stands next to the Shah and moves only one square diagonally. It became the queen of modern chess.
The French (1...e6) and the Caro-Kann (1...c6) work the same way: first a small pawn step, then ...d5 to challenge White's e4 pawn with two pawns.

The General (gung, said 'goong') is the piece you must protect. It shows 楚 for Cho and 漢 for Han. In the picture set it is a general wearing a helmet. It moves one point along any line of the palace, including the diagonals. From the center it can reach all 8 other points.

The General is the piece you must protect. Red's is 帥 (shuai, said 'shwhy') and Black's is 將 (jiang, said 'jyahng'). In the picture set it is a general wearing a helmet. It moves one point up, down, left or right, never diagonally, and it can never leave the palace.

The Gold General is 金将 (kin, said 'keen'). In the picture set it is a gold bar. It moves one square straight in any direction, or one square diagonally forward. It cannot go diagonally backward. That makes 6 squares.
The Horse is 傌 / 馬 (ma, said 'mah'). In the picture set it is a horse head. It moves one point straight, then one point diagonally outward. From the middle of the board it can reach up to 8 points.

The Horse 馬 (ma, said 'mah') moves one point straight and then one point diagonally outward, just like in xiangqi. In the picture set it is a horse head. If the first point is occupied, that way is blocked.
The Khon (said 'kohn') stands where the bishop stands in chess. It moves one square diagonally in any direction, or one square straight forward. In the picture set it is drawn like a bishop.
The Khun (said 'koon') is the king. In the picture set it is a king with a crown. It moves one square in any direction. There is no castling in makruk.
The king is the most important piece. If your king gets trapped, you lose! He moves just one square in any direction.

The King is 王将 / 玉将 (osho or gyokusho, said 'oh-show' / 'gyok-show'). In the picture set it is a king with a crown, and the little dots around the edge of every picture piece show where it can step. It moves one square in any direction.

The Knight is 桂馬 (keima, said 'kay-mah'). In the picture set it is a horse. It jumps two squares forward and one to the side, so it has only 2 squares to choose from. It jumps over pieces, but it can never move backward or sideways.
The knight moves in an L shape: two squares one way, then one square to the side.
The Lance is 香車 (kyosha, said 'kyoh-shah'), the Incense Chariot, drawn as a lance (a long spear). It moves any distance straight forward only. It can never turn around!
The London System is a setup you can play against almost anything: pawns on d4, e3, c3, bishop on f4, knights on f3 and d2. Get the bishop out before e3, or it gets locked in.
The Ma (said 'mah') is the horse. In the picture set it is a horse head. It moves exactly like a chess knight, in an L shape, and it can jump over pieces.
The Met (said 'met') stands where the queen stands in chess, but it is much weaker: it moves only one square diagonally. In the picture set it is a queen-like advisor.

The Pawn is 歩兵 (fu, said 'foo'), drawn as a foot soldier. It moves one square forward, and it also captures straight forward, not diagonally like in chess. Here your Pawn can take the black Pawn in front of it.
The queen goes on her own color: the white queen on a light square, the black queen on a dark square. The king takes the last spot.
The queen is the most powerful piece. She moves like a rook and a bishop: straight or diagonal, any distance.

The Rook is 飛車 (hisha, said 'hee-shah'), the Flying Chariot. It moves any distance straight, like a chess rook. The Bishop is 角行 (kaku, said 'kah-koo'), the Angle Mover. It moves any distance diagonally. Neither can jump. In the picture set they look like a chess rook and bishop.
The rook moves in straight lines: up, down, left or right, as far as it wants. The dots show where it can go.
The rooks go in the corners. Next to them are the knights, then the bishops.
The Rua (said 'roo-ah') means boat. In the picture set it is a boat. It moves like a chess rook: any distance straight. It is the strongest piece in makruk.

The Silver General is 銀将 (gin, said 'geen'). In the picture set it is a silver bar. It moves one square diagonally in any direction, or one square straight forward. It cannot move sideways or straight back. That makes 5 squares.
The Soldier is 兵 (bing, said 'bing') for Red and 卒 (zu, said 'dzoo') for Black. In the picture set it is a soldier with a spear. Before it crosses the river it can only move one point forward.

The Soldier is 兵 (byeong, said 'byuhng') for Cho and 卒 (jol, said 'jole') for Han. In the picture set it is a soldier with a spear. With no river in janggi, it may move one point forward or sideways from the very start. Never backward.

When a capture is possible, you must capture.
When a pawn reaches the other side of the board, it gets promoted! It turns into a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Usually a queen!
When a piece attacks the enemy king, it is called check. The king must get out of check right away!

When a piece captures, it explodes. The captured piece, the capturing piece, and every piece on the 8 squares around them are removed, except pawns (pawns only vanish if they capture or are captured themselves).

When they promote, these pieces get even stronger. The Dragon King 龍王 (ryuo, said 'ryoo-oh') moves like a Rook plus one square diagonally. The Dragon Horse 龍馬 (ryuma, said 'ryoo-mah') moves like a Bishop plus one square straight.
When two kings stand face to face with one square between them, they are in opposition. The side that does NOT have to move "has the opposition": the other king must step aside.
When White opens the center with d4, Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn. Black keeps two center pawns (d and e) against one, and the half-open c-file for a rook.
